quote: Bedingung dafür, dass umgekehrt ein System von linearen Transformationen von derart ist.
english: Condition for a system of linear transformations, conversely, to be of this kind.
topic: A sketch of how to obtain the invariants of a transformation group by expanding the transformation coefficients in power series of parameters, reducing to infinitesimal linear transformations, and seeking a linear invariant from which all invariants and their finiteness would follow.

triage.modern_statement: The page reduces a continuous transformation group to its infinitesimal (linear) transformations by expanding the coefficients in power series in the parameters. The note asks the converse: when does a given system of linear (infinitesimal) transformations actually come from such a group? In modern terms: which finite sets of linear vector fields or matrices are the infinitesimal generators of a Lie group of transformations? The answer is that their linear span must be closed under the commutator (Lie bracket), i.e. it must form a finite-dimensional Lie algebra. When that holds, the generators produce a local Lie group, or a simply connected global one.
triage.answered_by: Sophus Lie's fundamental theorems of transformation groups, in particular the converse of the first theorem and the second and third theorems. They were developed in the 1870s–1880s and set out in Lie–Engel, 'Theorie der Transformationsgruppen' (1888–1893). Later work completed the global form: every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of a simply connected Lie group (usually credited to Cartan). This attribution and dating come from my own knowledge; the sources found only state the theorems.

evidence.claim: Lie proved three theorems connecting Lie algebras and Lie groups. The third gives an equivalence between finite-dimensional real Lie algebras and local Lie groups.

A finite-dimensional Lie group of transformations is generated by its infinitesimal transformations. Conversely, any finite-dimensional Lie algebra of vector fields generates a Lie group (the first fundamental theorem).
Lie's third theorem: every finite-dimensional Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of a simply connected Lie group.
Classical Lie theory treats the 'group of infinitesimal transformations' attached to a continuous group, now read as its Lie algebra, together with Lie's three fundamental theorems.

triage.why: The page describes moving from a transformation group to its infinitesimal linear transformations. The natural reading of 'conversely' is the question of which systems of linear transformations arise this way, and Lie's theory answers it with the condition of closure under the bracket. That classical result was largely settled before or around the time of Hilbert's notebook. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th. Hilbert's 5th problem, about removing differentiability assumptions, is related but asks something different. Confidence is medium because the fragment is short: 'derart' might instead refer to some narrower property on the page, such as having a linear invariant, which would change exactly which result answers it. The search found no source that discusses this notebook entry itself.
